content: 1. Data integrity must be maintained to ensure that the information collected is consistent and accurate, avoiding any form of data corruption. 2. Accountability is essential, meaning that those responsible for collecting data must adhere to established principles and maintain confidentiality. 3. Patients with tuberculosis (TB) must have access to their complete health records, whether in paper or electronic format. 4. From an infection control perspective, individuals with infectious TB should not be transported until they have completed three months of treatment or are confirmed to no longer be infectious. 5. In exceptional cases, transporting an infectious TB patient may be considered, but only on carriers without other passengers and with feasible infection control measures in place. 6. Ground transportation, such as ambulances or private carriers, is preferred over air transport, even for short flights. 7. Managerial measures should include ensuring the availability of transportation equipped with infection control measures, pre-arranging detailed travel protocols with all stakeholders, and preparing all necessary travel and clinical documents for border authorities. 8. Administrative measures should aim to avoid delays in transportation, minimize public exposure in shared waiting areas, and provide comprehensive information to all personnel involved. 9. If non-recirculating ventilation is available, ensure maximum airflow from the vehicle's front to the rear, exiting through a rear window or exhaust fan. 10. If possible, physically isolate the driver’s cab from the rest of the vehicle, limit the number of passengers, and separate the patient from the driver. 11. The TB patient should wear a surgical mask that covers both the mouth and nose during transport. 12. Personnel involved in handling potentially infectious materials should wear particulate respirators and follow universal precautions, such as wearing gloves, disposing of materials in biohazard or sealed plastic bags, and avoiding aerosol generation of mycobacteria. 13. TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care are continuously updated as new tools, interventions, and evidence become available, aiming to achieve the End TB targets. 14. Systematic screening for TB should be expanded to include all at-risk populations, such as those previously treated for TB, individuals exposed to silica, those with untreated fibrotic lesions on chest radiography, and people with comorbidities like diabetes mellitus. 15. Screening should also target populations in correctional facilities, those affected by emergencies, and individuals from countries with a TB prevalence of 100 per 100,000 population or higher. 16. WHO recommends systematic TB screening for people living with HIV, household and close contacts of TB patients, and individuals in high-risk settings like prisons or workplaces with silica exposure. 17. Screening tools may include symptom checks, chest radiography, molecular diagnostic tests, and C-reactive protein testing for inflammation. 18. Contact tracing should involve interviewing TB patients to identify household and close contacts, with a focus on confidentiality and cultural sensitivity. 19. Contacts should be registered, evaluated, and provided with appropriate follow-up and treatment if necessary. 20. Health screening at points of entry or transit is recommended to identify individuals already on TB treatment or with other chronic conditions like HIV or diabetes. 21. Systematic TB screening should be conducted for all close contacts of TB patients and people living with HIV, with particular attention to vulnerable groups such as children under five years of age. 22. In stabilized emergency phases, TB screening should be expanded to include all at-risk populations, prioritizing those seeking healthcare and coming from high-prevalence regions. 23. Computer-aided detection software may be used to interpret digital chest radiography in place of human readers, improving screening and triage accuracy. 24. Rapid and accurate diagnostic tests, as well as drug susceptibility testing, are critical for effective TB management and should be accessible through a network of modern TB laboratories.
